name: Specific heat capacity
subject: Physics
aim: Find the specific heat capacity of a solid block by measuring the energy needed to raise its temperature.
outcome: c from the gradient of a temperature-against-energy graph, using E = mcΔθ.
safety: Heater and block stay hot after switch-off. Do not touch. Mop spills at once — mains electricity near water.
maths_link: Rearranging E = mcΔθ; gradient of a straight line; units.
notes: Thermal energy escaping is the main systematic error — always mention insulation in the evaluation.
topics: Energy, Rearranging Formulae, Straight Line Graphs, Units & Measures
equipment: Metal block with two holes (aluminium or copper)|Low-voltage immersion heater|Joulemeter (or ammeter, voltmeter and stopwatch)|Thermometer or temperature probe|Low-voltage power supply|Balance (0.1 g)|Insulation or lagging|Leads and crocodile clips|Small amount of water for the thermometer hole|Stopwatch
steps: Measure and record the mass of the block in kg. | Wrap the block in insulation and stand it on a heatproof mat. | Put the heater in the large hole and the thermometer in the small one, with a drop of water to improve contact. | Record the starting temperature. | Switch on and start timing. Record temperature and energy every minute for 10 minutes. | Switch off, but keep recording for two more minutes — the temperature keeps rising. | Plot temperature against energy supplied. | Gradient = 1/(mc), so c = 1/(m x gradient).
risks: The immersion heater and the block stay hot for minutes after the supply is off — leave them on the heatproof mat and do not lift the block until it is cool to the back of the hand. | Water in the thermometer hole beside a mains-fed supply — use the low-voltage supply only, and mop any spill before switching on. | Slotted block edges are sharp — carry it flat, not by the rim.
science: Energy going into the block does not vanish: it raises the average kinetic energy of the particles, which is what a thermometer reads as temperature. E = mcΔθ says how much, and c is the energy needed to raise one kilogram of the material by one degree — a property of the material, not of this block. Plot temperature against energy supplied and the gradient is 1/(mc), so a steep line means a material that heats easily. Two things about the shape are worth noticing: the line bends at the start, because the heater warms itself before it warms the block, and the temperature keeps climbing after switch-off, because energy is still travelling inwards from the heater.
log: Temperature every minute|Energy supplied, off the joulemeter or from power × time|The mass of the block, in kg|How far the temperature rises after the heater goes off
variables: The material of the block — aluminium against copper against steel|The mass of the block|The power of the heater|How well the block is insulated

name: Thermal insulation
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the thickness or type of material affects the rate at which water cools.
outcome: A cooling curve per material; the best insulator gives the smallest temperature drop.
safety: Hot water — use water no hotter than 80 C with under-14s. Carry the beaker with two hands.
maths_link: Rate of change; reading a curve; fair-test control variables.
notes: The one required practical that runs in a normal room. Same volume, same starting temperature, same lid every time.
equipment: Beaker (250 ml)|Kettle or hot water|Thermometer or temperature probe|Stopwatch|Insulating materials (bubble wrap, felt, newspaper, foam)|Lid with a hole|Measuring cylinder|Elastic bands|Ruler|Heatproof mat
steps: Wrap the beaker in one layer of the material and fix it with an elastic band. | Measure out the same volume of hot water each time. | Put the lid and thermometer in place and start the stopwatch. | Record the temperature every minute for 10 minutes. | Repeat with a second layer, then a third — or with a different material. | Plot all cooling curves on the same axes. | Compare the temperature drop over the full 10 minutes.
risks: Hot water scalds — the tutor fills the beaker, at no more than 80 °C for anyone under 14, and it is carried with two hands and set down before anyone else touches it. | A full beaker near the table edge — stand it at the back of the bench, away from bags and trailing sleeves. | A thermometer left standing in a beaker tips it — clamp it or hold it.
science: Hot water loses energy three ways at once: conduction through the beaker wall, convection in the air around it, and radiation from its surface. An insulator works mostly by trapping air — air is a poor conductor, and air that cannot move cannot convect — so what makes a good insulator is usually the pockets inside it rather than the material itself. That is why two thin layers often beat one thick one, and why the lid matters: the quickest route out of an open beaker is evaporation and convection off the top.
log: Temperature every minute for ten minutes|The total drop over the ten minutes|The time taken to fall by a fixed amount, say 10 °C|The shape of the cooling curve, not just its ends
variables: The material — bubble wrap, newspaper, felt, cotton wool|The number of layers|Whether the lid is on|The starting temperature of the water

name: Resistance of a wire
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length.
outcome: Resistance is directly proportional to length — a straight line through the origin.
safety: The wire gets hot. Keep the current low and disconnect between readings. Do not touch the wire while the circuit is on.
maths_link: R = V/I; direct proportion; line of best fit through the origin.
notes: Why current is kept low: a hot wire has a higher resistance, which bends the graph.
topics: Electricity, Straight Line Graphs, Direct Proportion
equipment: Nichrome wire (about 1 m, taped to a metre rule)|Metre rule|Crocodile clips|Ammeter|Voltmeter|Low-voltage power supply or battery pack|Switch|Connecting leads|Variable resistor|Heatproof mat
steps: Tape the wire alongside the metre rule. | Build a series circuit: supply, switch, ammeter, wire. Put the voltmeter across the wire. | Clip the crocodile clips 100 mm apart. | Close the switch, read current and potential difference, then open it again. | Repeat for 200, 300 ... up to 1000 mm. | Work out R = V/I for each length. | Plot resistance against length and draw a line of best fit.
risks: The nichrome wire gets hot enough to burn — keep the current low, open the switch between readings, and never touch the wire with the circuit closed. | The wire is taped to a metre rule and can spring loose — tape both ends and keep fingers off the free length. | A short circuit heats the leads — check the variable resistor is in before closing the switch.
science: A current is electrons drifting through a lattice of metal ions, and every collision with an ion transfers energy and slows them. A longer wire means more collisions, so doubling the length doubles the resistance — which is why the graph is a straight line through the origin rather than any other straight line. A thicker wire gives the electrons more routes side by side, so resistance falls as the cross-sectional area rises. Both are gathered into the resistivity in R = ρL/A. Keep the current small and open the switch between readings: a warm wire has a higher resistance, and that would bend the line.
log: The potential difference across the wire|The current through it|R = V/I at each length|The gradient of resistance against length
variables: The length of the wire|Its thickness — the SWG number|The material — constantan against copper against nichrome|The current, and so how warm the wire is allowed to get

name: I–V characteristics
subject: Physics
aim: Find the current–potential difference graphs for a resistor, a filament lamp and a diode.
outcome: Straight line for the resistor, S-curve for the lamp, one-way step for the diode.
safety: Do not exceed the component ratings. The lamp gets hot.
maths_link: Gradient and its reciprocal; interpreting non-linear graphs.
notes: The diode always needs a protective resistor in series or it burns out.
equipment: Fixed resistor|Filament lamp|Diode|Protective resistor for the diode|Ammeter|Voltmeter|Variable resistor|Low-voltage power supply|Switch|Connecting leads
steps: Build a series circuit with the component, ammeter, variable resistor and supply. | Connect the voltmeter across the component only. | Set the variable resistor to its highest value and close the switch. | Record current and potential difference, then adjust and repeat for about eight settings. | Reverse the supply connections and repeat for negative values. | Swap in the next component and repeat. | Plot I against V for all three on separate axes.
risks: The filament lamp gets hot — let it cool before moving it, and do not exceed the rating printed on it. | A diode without its protective resistor burns out and can get hot — put the resistor in the circuit before the supply goes on. | Leads warm if the current is pushed up — work inside the component ratings and open the switch between readings.
science: A fixed resistor held at one temperature obeys Ohm's law, so the current is proportional to the potential difference and the graph is a straight line through the origin. A filament lamp does not: the current heats the filament, a hotter filament resists more, so the line flattens as the voltage rises — the curve is the resistance changing underneath you. A diode conducts one way: almost nothing flows below about 0.7 V, then the current climbs steeply, and in reverse it stays near zero. The gradient of an I–V graph is 1/R, so a curve that flattens is a resistance that is rising.
log: The current at each setting|The potential difference at each setting|The gradient, and so the resistance, at several points along each curve|The voltage at which the diode starts to conduct
variables: The component — resistor, filament lamp, diode|The potential difference, set by the variable resistor|Which way round the supply is connected|Whether the lamp is given time to cool between readings

name: Density
subject: Physics
aim: Measure the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids.
outcome: ρ = m/V for each sample; the displacement method for anything awkwardly shaped.
safety: Water and balances — wipe up spills. Take care with the eureka can spout.
maths_link: Rearranging formulas; unit conversion between g/cm3 and kg/m3.
notes: Runs perfectly well on a library table. The scales (I030) and ruler are already on the items list.
topics: Particle Model of Matter, Compound Measures, Rearranging Formulae, Units & Measures
equipment: Balance (0.01 g if possible)|Measuring cylinder|Eureka (displacement) can|Beaker|Water|Regular solids (cube, cylinder)|Irregular solids (stone, key, modelling clay)|Liquid samples|30 cm ruler|Paper towel
steps: Measure the mass of the object. | For a regular solid, measure its dimensions and calculate the volume. | For an irregular solid, fill the eureka can to the spout and let it settle. | Lower the object in gently and collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder. | Read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level. | For a liquid, find the mass of an empty cylinder, add the liquid, and find the mass again. | Calculate ρ = m/V and compare with published values.
risks: Water and a balance together — wipe every spill at once, and keep the balance on a dry part of the bench. | The eureka can spout drips onto the floor — stand it over a tray and put the catch beaker under the spout before filling. | Dropping a stone into a measuring cylinder cracks the base — lower it down a tilted cylinder rather than dropping it.
science: Density is how much mass is packed into a given volume, ρ = m/V, and it belongs to the material rather than to the lump: half a brick has half the mass and half the volume and exactly the same density. Volume is the awkward half. A cuboid can be measured and multiplied out; anything irregular has to be found by displacement, because an object lowered into a full container pushes aside precisely its own volume of water. A liquid cannot be weighed without something to hold it, so its mass is found by difference. 1 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³, and that conversion is where most of the marks go.

variables: The material of the sample|Whether the shape is regular or irregular|The method used for the volume — calculated, or by displacement|The size of the sample, which should not change the answer at all

name: Force and extension (Hooke’s law)
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied.
outcome: A straight line up to the limit of proportionality; spring constant from the gradient.
safety: Wear eye protection. Put a mat or tray under the masses, and never stand with feet under the hanger.
maths_link: F = ke; gradient; identifying where a linear model breaks down.
notes: A brilliant demonstration of "the maths only works in a range".
topics: Forces, Straight Line Graphs, Direct Proportion
equipment: Spring|Clamp stand, boss and clamp|30 cm ruler or metre rule|Slotted masses and hanger (100 g) × about 8|Pointer or pin|Eye protection|Soft mat or tray|G-clamp to secure the stand|Balance|Graph paper
steps: Clamp the stand to the bench and hang the spring from it. | Record the unloaded length of the spring against the ruler. | Add a 100 g mass and record the new length once it stops moving. | Repeat, adding masses one at a time, up to about eight. | Extension = loaded length minus original length. | Force = mass in kg x 9.8. | Plot force against extension and find the gradient — that is the spring constant. | Note where the line stops being straight: the limit of proportionality.
risks: A spring under load can snap and fly — eye protection on before the first mass goes on, and nobody leans over the hanger. | Falling masses land on feet — put a soft mat or tray under the hanger and keep feet out from under it. | The clamp stand topples as the load grows — G-clamp the base to the bench before loading.
science: A spring stretches because the forces between its atoms resist being pulled apart, and for small extensions that resistance is proportional to how far you have pulled: F = ke, with k the spring constant in newtons per metre. A stiff spring has a large k and therefore a shallow line on an extension-against-force graph. Past the limit of proportionality the line bends, because the coils start to straighten out rather than the whole spring flexing; past the elastic limit the spring does not come back to its original length at all. Extension is the CHANGE in length, never the length itself — which is the commonest lost mark on this practical.
log: The length of the spring at each load|The extension, as length minus original length|The gradient of force against extension, which is k|The load at which the line stops being straight
variables: The force added, in 100 g steps|The spring itself — a stiff one against a soft one|Two springs end to end, or two side by side|How far past the straight part you are willing to go

name: Force and acceleration
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how acceleration depends on force and on mass.
outcome: a is proportional to F for a fixed mass, and inversely proportional to m for a fixed force.
safety: Catch the falling masses — do not let them land on feet. Clamp the pulley firmly.
maths_link: Direct and inverse proportion; F = ma.
notes: The mass is moved, not added, so total mass stays constant. Examiners ask this constantly.
topics: Forces, Direct Proportion, Inverse Proportion, Substitution
equipment: Dynamics trolley|Runway or smooth bench|Pulley and clamp|String|Slotted masses and hanger|Light gates and datalogger (or ticker tape and timer)|Balance|Metre rule|Stopwatch|Soft landing box
steps: Set up the runway with the pulley at one end and the landing box beneath it. | Tilt the runway slightly to compensate for friction until the trolley moves at a steady speed when nudged. | Attach the string from the trolley over the pulley to the hanger. | Keep the total mass constant: move masses from the trolley to the hanger, not on to it. | Release the trolley and record the acceleration from the light gates. | Repeat for a range of accelerating forces. | Then keep the force constant and add mass to the trolley instead. | Plot a against F, and a against 1/m.
risks: The falling mass hanger lands on feet — put a soft landing under it and keep the floor clear. | The trolley runs off the end of the runway — put a catcher or a block at the far end before the first run. | The pulley pulls loose under load — clamp it firmly and check it after every few runs.
science: F = ma says the acceleration is set by the resultant force and by the mass being accelerated. Hold the mass constant and double the force and the acceleration doubles — a straight line through the origin. Hold the force constant and double the mass and the acceleration halves, which is a curve against m and a straight line against 1/m. The mass being accelerated is the trolley AND the hanging masses together, which is why they are moved from one to the other rather than added: adding them would change the force and the mass in the same breath. Tilting the runway cancels friction, so the string tension is the only resultant force left.
log: The acceleration from the light gates|The velocity at each gate|The accelerating force in newtons|a against F, and a against 1/m
variables: The accelerating force — how many masses hang on the end|The total mass being accelerated|The tilt of the runway, and so how much friction is cancelled|The surface of the runway

name: Waves
subject: Physics
aim: Measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and on a string.
outcome: v = f λ verified in two different media.
safety: Water and mains electricity — use a low-voltage supply. Warn anyone photosensitive before using a strobe.
maths_link: v = f λ; measuring ten and dividing to reduce error.
notes: Filming on a phone at 240 fps replaces the strobe and is usually easier.
equipment: Ripple tank with lamp|Signal generator and vibration generator|Strobe light or video camera|White card or paper for the screen|30 cm ruler|Metre rule|String|Pulley and slotted masses|Clamp stand|Stopwatch

Calculate v again.

science: A wave carries energy without carrying matter: the water in the ripple tank bobs up and down and stays where it is. The frequency is how many wavefronts pass a point each second and is set by the dipper; the wavelength is the distance between two crests and is set by the frequency and the medium together. v = fλ ties the three, and the speed belongs to the MEDIUM — change the depth of the water and the speed changes, so the wavelength changes while the frequency stays wherever the generator put it. On a string the wave reflects off both ends and interferes with itself, which is why only certain frequencies give a clear standing wave and why the wavelength is twice the distance between adjacent nodes.

name: Light: reflection and refraction
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate reflection at a mirror and refraction through a glass block.
outcome: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; the ray bends towards the normal entering glass.
safety: The ray box lamp gets hot. Dim the room but keep walkways clear.
maths_link: Angle measurement; the normal as a reference line; ratios.
notes: Needs only a ray box on top of what is already on the items list. A protractor (I006) is essential.
equipment: Ray box with a single slit|Rectangular glass block|Plane mirror|Protractor|30 cm ruler|Plain A4 paper|Sharp pencil|Power supply for the ray box|Blu-tack|Darkened area of the room
steps: Put the paper down and draw round the block or mirror. | Draw the normal at 90 degrees to the surface where the ray will enter. | Shine a single ray at the surface at about 30 degrees to the normal. | Mark the incoming ray with two crosses and the outgoing ray with two more. | Remove the block and join the crosses to reconstruct the ray path. | Measure the angles of incidence, reflection and refraction from the normal. | Repeat for 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees. | Tabulate and look for the pattern.
risks: The ray box lamp gets hot enough to burn — let it cool before moving it, and keep paper off the housing. | A dimmed room is a trip hazard — clear bags and stools from the walkway before the lights go down. | The glass block chips and cuts if it is dropped — slide it on the paper rather than lifting it across the bench.
science: Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium and changes direction at a boundary. At a mirror it reflects, angle of incidence equal to angle of reflection — both measured from the normal, the line at 90° to the surface, and never from the surface itself. At glass it refracts, because light travels more slowly in glass: going in, the ray bends towards the normal; coming out, it bends away by the same amount, so a rectangular block shifts a ray sideways without changing the direction it ends up travelling. Past a critical angle nothing leaves at all and the light is totally internally reflected, which is how a fibre-optic cable works.

name: Infrared radiation
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the surface of an object affects the infrared radiation it emits or absorbs.
outcome: Matt black emits and absorbs most; shiny silver least.
safety: Boiling water inside the cube. Fill it carefully and do not move it once filled.
maths_link: Means; controlling distance as a variable.
notes: An infrared thermometer from a hardware shop is a cheap substitute for a thermopile.

science: Every object above absolute zero emits infrared, and how much depends on its temperature and on its surface. Matt black is the best emitter and the best absorber; shiny silver is the worst at both. Colour and texture are doing separate jobs — matt black and shiny black differ, so it is not only the colour — and the same surface that emits well absorbs well, which is why the two halves of this practical give the same ranking. name: Making a soluble salt
subject: Chemistry
aim: Prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate and an acid.
outcome: Blue copper sulfate crystals, filtered and left to crystallise.
safety: Dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant — goggles throughout. Hot evaporating basins and Bunsen flames.
maths_link: Excess reagent; percentage yield.
notes: Slow crystallisation gives bigger, better crystals. Heating to dryness ruins them.
equipment: Dilute sulfuric acid × 25 cm3|Copper(II) oxide powder|250 ml beaker|Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze, heatproof mat|Spatula|Stirring rod|Filter funnel and filter paper|Conical flask|Evaporating basin|Eye protection
steps: Put 25 cm3 of dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker and warm it gently. Do not boil. | Turn off the Bunsen and add copper oxide a spatula at a time, stirring. | Keep adding until no more dissolves and some solid stays at the bottom — the acid is now used up. | Filter the mixture to remove the excess copper oxide. | Pour the blue filtrate into an evaporating basin. | Heat gently to concentrate it, stopping when crystals start to form at the edge. | Leave to crystallise slowly, then pat the crystals dry between filter papers.
risks: Dilute sulfuric acid irritates skin and eyes — goggles from before the bottle is opened until the bench is cleared, and any splash is washed off at once. | The evaporating basin and the tripod stay hot long after the flame is out — leave them on the mat and check with the back of a hand. | Bunsen flame and loose hair or sleeves — hair tied back, sleeves up, flame on the yellow safety flame between heatings. | Boiling the solution to dryness spits hot crystals — stop heating while liquid is still visible and let the last of it evaporate on its own.
science: An acid and an insoluble base give a salt and water: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Adding the base in excess is the trick of it — once no more will dissolve, every bit of acid has reacted, so what is left in solution is the salt and nothing else, and the filter takes the leftover base away. Crystals form because the solution becomes saturated as water evaporates, and the slower they are left to grow the larger and better formed they are, since the ions have time to find their places in the lattice. Heating to dryness drives off the water of crystallisation and leaves a white powder where the blue crystals should be.

aim: Find the volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali.
outcome: Concordant titres within 0.10 cm3, and a concentration calculated from them.

notes: The single most transferable maths practical in chemistry — good for a Higher-tier student who needs moles practice.

name: Electrolysis
subject: Chemistry
aim: Investigate what is produced at each electrode when aqueous solutions are electrolysed.
outcome: Metal or hydrogen at the cathode, halogen or oxygen at the anode, predicted from the reactivity series.
safety: Chlorine gas — use a fume cupboard or a very small volume in a well-ventilated room. Goggles throughout.
maths_link: Half equations; balancing charge.
notes: Must be d.c. Alternating current gives nothing useful and confuses the write-up.
equipment: Electrolysis cell or 100 ml beaker|Graphite (carbon) electrodes × 2|Low-voltage d.c. power supply|Connecting leads and crocodile clips|Copper(II) sulfate solution|Sodium chloride solution|Test tubes for collecting gas|Wooden splints|Blue litmus paper|Eye protection
steps: Half-fill the cell with copper sulfate solution. | Clamp the two graphite electrodes so they do not touch. | Connect to the d.c. supply at about 4 V and switch on. | Watch both electrodes: note any coating, bubbling or colour change. | Test any gas — a glowing splint relights in oxygen; damp litmus is bleached by chlorine. | Switch off, rinse everything and repeat with sodium chloride solution. | Write half equations for each electrode.
risks: Chlorine comes off the positive electrode from sodium chloride solution — a fume cupboard, or a very small volume with the window open, and nobody sniffs the cell. | Copper(II) sulfate solution is harmful if swallowed and stains — goggles on, hands washed before anyone leaves. | Graphite electrodes crumble and short across the cell — check they are clear of each other before the supply goes on. | Low-voltage supply near an open cell of solution — the supply stands away from the beaker and is switched off before anything is moved.
science: A current splits an ionic compound into its elements. Positive ions travel to the negative cathode and gain electrons; negative ions travel to the positive anode and lose them. Which product actually appears is a competition. At the cathode the metal is deposited if it is less reactive than hydrogen, and hydrogen comes off if it is not; at the anode a halogen is released if one is there, and oxygen from the water if not. That is why copper sulfate gives copper and oxygen while sodium chloride gives hydrogen and chlorine — the water is a reactant here, not just something the salt is dissolved in.

name: Temperature changes
subject: Chemistry
aim: Investigate the temperature change when acid reacts with alkali in different proportions.
outcome: A peak temperature at the neutralisation point.
safety: Dilute acid and alkali — goggles and no skin contact. Use low concentrations with younger students.
maths_link: Reading a maximum from a graph; interpolation.
notes: Exothermic and endothermic made visible. Works on a library table with cheap kit.
equipment: Polystyrene cup|Second cup or beaker for insulation|Lid with a hole|Thermometer or temperature probe|Measuring cylinders (25 cm3) × 2|Dilute hydrochloric acid × 30 cm3|Sodium hydroxide solution × 40 cm3|Stopwatch|Stirring rod|Eye protection

risks: Dilute acid and alkali splash when they are poured together — goggles on both of you, and the lower concentrations for anyone younger. | The cup tips as the thermometer goes in — stand the polystyrene cup inside a beaker before anything is added. | The mixture warms enough to surprise a hand on the cup — hold the outer beaker rather than the cup.
science: Neutralisation is exothermic: making the O–H bonds in water releases more energy than it takes to break the bonds in the acid and the alkali, and the difference warms the mixture. Each 5 cm³ of alkali neutralises a little more acid and releases a little more energy, so the temperature climbs — until the acid runs out. After that the alkali going in is cold liquid diluting a warm mixture, so the temperature falls again. The peak is therefore the neutralisation point, and it is read off where the two straight parts of the graph would meet rather than off the highest dot, which is as likely to be a stray reading as the true maximum.

name: Rates of reaction
subject: Chemistry
aim: Investigate how concentration affects the rate of a reaction, by two different methods.
outcome: Rate increases with concentration; a 1/time graph against concentration.
safety: Sulfur dioxide is produced in the thiosulfate method — ventilate the room and keep volumes small. Goggles throughout.
maths_link: Rate as 1/time; proportionality; controlling total volume.
notes: Everyone judges "disappeared" slightly differently — same person watching every run.
topics: Rate of Reaction, Real-Life Graphs, Direct Proportion
equipment: Sodium thiosulfate solution|Dilute hydrochloric acid|Conical flask|Paper with a black cross drawn on it|Stopwatch|Measuring cylinders|Distilled water for dilutions|Gas syringe (for the marble chip method)|Marble chips|Eye protection
steps: Draw a black cross on paper and stand the flask on it. | Measure 50 cm3 of thiosulfate into the flask. | Add 10 cm3 of acid and start the stopwatch at the moment of mixing. | Look down through the flask and stop the clock when the cross disappears. | Repeat with the thiosulfate diluted — 40 cm3 solution to 10 cm3 water, and so on. | Keep the total volume the same every time. | Plot 1/time against concentration.
risks: Sulfur dioxide comes off the thiosulfate and acid mixture and irritates the airway — keep volumes small, ventilate the room, and take the flask away to a sink at the end rather than leaving it open on the bench. | Anyone asthmatic is at more risk from that gas than the rest of the room — ask first, and run the gas-syringe version with them instead. | Dilute hydrochloric acid on skin — goggles throughout and wash a splash off at once.
science: A reaction happens when particles collide hard enough and the right way round. A more concentrated solution has more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent and the rate goes up. Thiosulfate and acid give sulfur, which clouds the mixture, so the time for the cross to disappear measures the rate — and because a slow reaction takes LONGER, the rate is 1/time rather than time. The total volume is kept the same by swapping solution for water: diluting by adding extra liquid would change the depth the light has to travel through as well, which would alter the result for a reason that has nothing to do with rate.

subject: Chemistry
aim: Separate the dyes in inks and calculate Rf values.

notes: No lab needed. Rf is a good ratio exercise for a student who finds ratio abstract.

steps: Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of the paper. Pencil, never pen. | Spot each ink on the line, letting each spot dry before adding more. | Pour water into the beaker to a depth of about 1 cm. | Hang the paper so the bottom edge is in the water but the pencil line is above it. | Cover with the watch glass and leave undisturbed. | Remove the paper before the solvent front reaches the top, and mark the front immediately. | Measure the distance moved by each spot and by the solvent front. | Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front.

science: Chromatography separates a mixture by giving each component a choice between two phases: the solvent moving up the paper, and the paper itself. A dye that dissolves well and clings to the paper weakly travels a long way; one that clings tightly hardly moves. Rf is the ratio of how far the spot went to how far the solvent went, so it always comes out between 0 and 1, and it is the same for a given dye and solvent whatever size the paper is — which is what makes it worth quoting at all. The line is pencil because ink would run with everything else, and the paper must not dip below it, or the spots dissolve straight into the water.

name: Identifying ions
subject: Chemistry
aim: Use flame tests and chemical tests to identify metal ions and non-metal ions.
outcome: A flame colour and a precipitate colour for each unknown.
safety: Bunsen flames and concentrated-ish solutions. Goggles, tied hair, no loose sleeves.
maths_link: Systematic elimination; reading a results table.
notes: Flame tests are the memorable bit. The hydroxide precipitates carry more marks.
equipment: Bunsen burner and heatproof mat|Nichrome wire loop or wooden splints|Dilute hydrochloric acid for cleaning the loop|Samples of metal salts|Sodium hydroxide solution|Test tubes and rack|Dropping pipettes|Limewater|Silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid|Eye protection
steps: Clean the wire loop in acid and hold it in a blue flame until no colour shows. | Dip it in the sample and hold it at the edge of a blue flame. | Record the colour: lithium red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green. | For metal hydroxide tests, add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to the sample in a test tube. | Record the precipitate colour, then add excess to see if it redissolves. | For carbonates, add acid and bubble the gas through limewater. | Match the results against a table of known ions.
risks: Bunsen flame with a wire loop held in it — hair tied back, sleeves up, and the loop goes into the flame away from everybody rather than across the bench. | The nichrome loop stays red-hot and looks cold — it is rested on the mat between samples and never put down on the bench. | Sodium hydroxide solution is corrosive to eyes — goggles throughout, added dropwise down the side of the tube. | Cleaning the loop in hydrochloric acid spits when it goes back into the flame — shake the drop off before returning it.
science: A flame test works because the heat lifts an atom's outer electrons to a higher level; they fall back and give out the difference as light, and the size of that gap is fixed for each metal, so the colour names it. The hydroxide tests work on a different principle: sodium hydroxide makes insoluble metal hydroxides whose colours differ — copper blue, iron(II) green, iron(III) brown. Aluminium's white precipitate redissolves in excess where calcium's and magnesium's do not, and that is how those three are told apart. The loop is cleaned between samples because a trace of sodium gives a yellow bright enough to hide everything else.

outcome: A pH, a mass of dissolved solids, and pure distilled water from a salty sample.
safety: Hot glassware and boiling water. Anti-bumping granules in the flask. Never seal the apparatus.
maths_link: Mass by difference; concentration in g per dm3.
notes: Ties neatly to a walk to the nearest pond — pond, tap and bottled water side by side.

science: Fresh water from any source is not pure: it carries dissolved salts, and the mass left behind after evaporation says how much. Distillation separates by boiling point: the water boils off, travels through the condenser, cools back to a liquid and leaves everything with a higher boiling point behind, which is why the distillate leaves no residue when it is evaporated in turn. The thermometer bulb sits level with the side arm because what it has to measure is the vapour going over, not the liquid in the flask.

name: Microscopy
subject: Biology
aim: Use a light microscope to observe and draw plant or animal cells, and calculate magnification.
outcome: A labelled biological drawing with a magnification and a real size calculation.
safety: Coverslips and slides break and cut. Mounted needles are sharp. No cheek cells without a risk assessment.
maths_link: Standard form; unit conversion mm to μm; rearranging.
notes: A basic school microscope is around £60 and turns this into something you can run anywhere.
topics: Cell Biology, Standard Form, Units & Measures, Rearranging Formulae
equipment: Light microscope|Microscope slides|Coverslips|Onion or prepared slides|Iodine stain|Mounted needle|Forceps|Dropping pipette|Paper towel|Pencil and plain paper for the drawing
steps: Peel a thin layer of onion epidermis with forceps. | Lay it flat on a slide and add one drop of iodine. | Lower the coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles. | Start on the lowest objective lens and focus with the coarse focus. | Switch to a higher objective and use the fine focus only. | Draw what you see with clean, single pencil lines and no shading. | Magnification = eyepiece x objective. | Real size = image size / magnification. Watch the units.
risks: Coverslips and slides break into small sharp pieces — lower the coverslip with a mounted needle, and sweep breakages into the sharps bin rather than picking them up. | The mounted needle is sharp — it is pointed away from the hand holding the slide. | Iodine stain marks skin and clothes and irritates eyes — one drop from a pipette, goggles on. | Cheek cells are a human-tissue risk assessment of their own — onion only, unless that assessment has been done.
science: A light microscope uses two lenses: the objective makes a magnified real image and the eyepiece magnifies that again, so the total magnification is the two multiplied together. What limits it is not magnification but RESOLUTION — how close two things can be and still look like two — and for light that is about 200 nm, set by the wavelength, which is why an electron microscope is needed for anything smaller than an organelle. Iodine stains the starch and the cell wall so the outlines show; unstained, an onion cell is nearly transparent. Real size = image size ÷ magnification, and almost every mark lost here is a unit: 1 mm is 1000 μm.

name: Microbiology
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of antiseptics or antibiotics on bacterial growth.
outcome: Clear zones of inhibition, measured and compared as areas.
safety: Strict aseptic technique. Incubate at 25 C maximum in a school, and never reopen a sealed plate.
maths_link: Area of a circle; comparing areas rather than diameters.
notes: Genuinely needs a school or college lab. Not one to run at a library.
topics: Infection & Response, Area & Circumference of Circles
equipment: Sterile agar plates|Bacterial culture (E. coli or B. subtilis)|Sterile pipette|Inoculating loop|Bunsen burner|Sterile paper discs|Antiseptics and antibiotics|Sticky tape|Incubator set to 25 C|30 cm ruler
steps: Sterilise the inoculating loop in a blue flame until red hot, then let it cool. | Spread the bacterial culture evenly across the agar surface. | Place the paper discs, each soaked in a different antiseptic, on the agar with sterile forceps. | Include a disc soaked in sterile water as the control. | Tape the lid on in two places — never seal it all the way round. | Incubate upside down at 25 C for 48 hours. | Measure the diameter of each clear zone and calculate its area with πr2.
risks: Live bacterial culture — strict aseptic technique, the plate is taped shut in two places and never reopened. | Incubating above 25 °C in a school selects for organisms that grow at body temperature — the incubator is set to 25 °C and checked before the plates go in. | The inoculating loop is flamed red-hot and stays hot — it is cooled in the agar edge before it touches the culture. | Used plates are a disposal hazard — autoclaved or sealed for collection, never in the ordinary bin.
science: Bacteria grow outwards from wherever they were spread, and an antiseptic that reaches them stops them dividing — so a clear ring appears round the disc where nothing has grown. How big that ring is depends on how effective the antiseptic is and on how far it diffuses through the agar. Area is the fair comparison rather than diameter, because doubling the diameter quadruples the area, and a ranking by diameter understates the difference. The water disc is the control: without it a clear zone could be the paper blocking growth rather than what is on it. The lid is taped in two places so air can reach the plate, and it is incubated at 25 °C rather than body temperature, both to keep human pathogens from growing.

variables: The antiseptic or antibiotic on the disc|Its concentration|The species of bacteria|The incubation temperature and time

name: Osmosis
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of sugar solution concentration on the mass of potato tissue.
outcome: A percentage change in mass graph crossing zero at the cell sap concentration.
safety: Cork borers and scalpels are sharp — cut on a board, away from the body. Adult supervision for under-14s.
maths_link: Percentage change; reading an intercept; why percentages beat raw change.
notes: Blotting technique is the biggest source of error — same number of dabs every time.
topics: Cell Biology, Percentage Increase & Decrease, Straight Line Graphs
equipment: Potato|Cork borer|Scalpel or knife and cutting board|30 cm ruler|Balance (0.01 g)|Sucrose solutions of 0.0 to 1.0 mol/dm3 × 5|Boiling tubes and rack|Paper towel|Marker pen|Stopwatch or timer
steps: Bore five cylinders from the same potato and trim them all to the same length. | Blot each one dry and record its starting mass. | Put one cylinder in each concentration and note the time. | Leave for at least 30 minutes — overnight is better. | Remove, blot dry the same way as before, and reweigh. | Percentage change = (change in mass / starting mass) x 100. | Plot percentage change against concentration and read off where the line crosses zero.
risks: Cork borers and scalpels cut to the bone — cut down onto a board, away from the body, and nobody else's hand is near the board. | A cork borer twisted through a potato slips when it breaks through — the potato is flat on the board and the borer is turned rather than pushed. | Sucrose solutions spilled on the floor are sticky and slippery — the rack stands in a tray. | Under-14s with a scalpel — the tutor does the cutting, the student measures.
science: Osmosis is water moving through a partially permeable membrane from where water is more concentrated to where it is less. A potato cylinder in pure water takes water in and gains mass; in strong sugar solution it loses both. Somewhere between, the solution matches the cell sap and nothing moves either way — that is where the line crosses zero, and finding it is the reason the graph is worth plotting instead of just listing the masses. Percentage change is used rather than raw change because the cylinders do not start at identical masses, and 0.2 g means something different on a 2 g cylinder than on a 4 g one.
log: The mass before and after|The percentage change in mass|The concentration at which the line crosses zero|How firm each cylinder feels at the end
variables: The concentration of the sugar solution|The tissue — potato, sweet potato, beetroot|The time left in the solution|The surface area of the cylinder

name: Food tests
subject: Biology
aim: Use qualitative reagents to test for starch, sugars, proteins and lipids.
outcome: Four colour changes, each identifying one food group.
safety: Benedict’s needs a hot water bath, not a naked flame. Ethanol is highly flammable — no Bunsen anywhere near it. Check food allergies before handling any sample.
maths_link: Qualitative versus quantitative data.
notes: Check allergies before this one, always. The lipid test uses ethanol, so it is lab-only.
equipment: Test tubes and rack|Benedict’s solution|Iodine solution|Biuret reagent|Ethanol|Water bath at 75 C|Pestle and mortar|Filter funnel and paper|Dropping pipettes|Food samples
steps: Grind the food with a little distilled water and filter it. | Starch: add a few drops of iodine. Orange to blue-black is positive. | Sugars: add Benedict’s and stand in the hot water bath for five minutes. Blue to brick red is positive. | Protein: add Biuret reagent. Blue to purple is positive. | Lipids: shake the sample with ethanol, then pour into water. A cloudy white emulsion is positive. | Record the starting and finishing colour for every test — not just the result.
risks: Ethanol is highly flammable and its vapour travels — no Bunsen, no flame anywhere in the room while the bottle is open, and the water bath is electric. | Benedict's solution is harmful and the bath is at 75 °C — goggles, and tubes are lifted with a holder rather than fingers. | Biuret reagent contains sodium hydroxide and is corrosive to eyes — goggles throughout, added dropwise. | Food samples carry allergens — check every allergy in the room before a single sample is opened, and nothing is tasted.
science: Each reagent reacts with one class of molecule and reports it as a colour. Iodine goes blue-black with starch because the iodine sits inside the coiled starch chain. Benedict's needs heat and goes brick red with reducing sugars, as copper(II) is reduced to copper(I) oxide. Biuret goes purple with the peptide bonds in protein — so it is testing for the bond rather than for any particular protein. The ethanol emulsion test works because lipids dissolve in ethanol and not in water, so tipping the ethanol into water throws them out of solution as a cloud of droplets. All four are QUALITATIVE: they say whether, not how much.

variables: The food being tested|The concentration of the food solution|Whether the sample is ground and filtered first|The time in the water bath, for Benedict's

name: Enzymes
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch.
outcome: A rate-against-pH curve with an optimum.
safety: Iodine stains skin and clothes. Goggles. Buffer solutions are irritants.
maths_link: Rate as a reciprocal of time; identifying an optimum from a curve.
notes: Keep the temperature constant with a water bath — otherwise two variables change at once.
equipment: Amylase solution|Starch solution|Buffer solutions from pH 4 to pH 10|Spotting tile|Iodine solution|Dropping pipettes|Stopwatch|Water bath at 35 C|Test tubes|Stirring rod
steps: Put a drop of iodine in every well of the spotting tile. | Mix 2 cm3 starch, 2 cm3 amylase and 2 cm3 of one buffer in a test tube. Start the stopwatch. | Every 30 seconds, take a drop of the mixture and add it to the next iodine well. | Blue-black means starch is still present. Keep going until the drop stays orange. | Record the time taken for the starch to disappear. | Repeat for each pH. | Rate = 1000 / time. Plot rate against pH.
risks: Iodine solution stains skin and clothes and irritates eyes — goggles, and it goes onto the tile from a pipette rather than being poured. | Buffer solutions are irritants — goggles, and hands washed before leaving. | A 35 °C water bath with tubes in it tips if it is knocked — it sits at the back of the bench with the leads behind it.
science: Amylase breaks starch down into maltose, and it does it at an active site shaped to fit the starch. pH changes the charges on the amino acids that hold that shape, so too far either side of the optimum and the active site no longer fits — the enzyme is denatured, and that change does not reverse when the pH is put back. Iodine is the reporter: while starch is there the drop goes blue-black, and the moment it stays orange the starch has gone. A faster reaction takes less time, so the rate is 1000/time, and plotting that against pH gives a curve with a clear peak rather than a trough.

name: Photosynthesis
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.
outcome: Rate against 1/d2, showing the inverse square relationship.
safety: Lamp and water together — keep the supply away from the beaker. The lamp gets hot.
maths_link: Inverse square law; means; why 1/d2 straightens the graph.
notes: The heat shield is what stops temperature becoming a second variable.

science: Photosynthesis uses light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, and the bubbles are that oxygen. More light means more energy arriving, so the rate rises — until something else runs short and the graph levels off, at which point carbon dioxide or temperature has become the limiting factor. Light from a lamp spreads out over the surface of a sphere, so its intensity falls with the square of the distance; plotting rate against 1/d² straightens the curve and shows the proportionality directly. The beaker of water in the way absorbs infrared, so moving the lamp changes the light without changing the temperature.

name: Reaction time
subject: Biology
aim: Measure the effect of a factor on human reaction time.
outcome: A mean reaction time in seconds, before and after the factor changes.
safety: None beyond the obvious. Do not test caffeine on under-16s.
maths_link: Means; converting a distance to a time; anomalies.
notes: Zero kit beyond a ruler. The best required practical for a first session with a nervous student.
equipment: 30 cm ruler|Chair and table|A partner|Conversion table or the formula t = √(2d/g)|Calculator|Results table|Stopwatch (for the computer version)|Tablet or laptop with a reaction-time test|Pen|Whiteboard for class results
steps: Sit with your forearm flat on the table and your hand over the edge, thumb and finger 1 cm apart. | Your partner holds the ruler with the zero mark level with your thumb. | They drop it without warning; you catch it as fast as you can. | Record the number the top of your thumb lands on. | Repeat ten times and discard the first two attempts as practice. | Convert distance to time using t = √(2d/g). | Change one factor — a distraction, background noise — and repeat.
risks: Almost nothing physical — the one thing to set is that the dropped ruler is caught rather than grabbed at, so nobody bangs a hand on the table edge. | Testing the effect of caffeine on anyone under 16 is not done at all — the comparison is between people, or between hands.
science: A reflex misses the brain out, but catching a ruler does not: light reaches the eye, a signal goes to the brain, the brain decides, and a signal travels down the arm — so what is being measured is the whole loop, which is why it comes out in hundreds of milliseconds rather than the few a spinal reflex takes. The ruler is the clock: a dropped object falls d = ½gt², so the distance it fell before you caught it converts to a time, t = √(2d/g). The first attempts are thrown away because people get noticeably better within a few goes, and that improvement would otherwise look like an effect of whatever you changed.

name: Plant responses and germination
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of light or gravity on the growth of newly germinated seedlings.
outcome: Shoots bend towards light; roots grow downwards regardless of orientation.
safety: Wash hands after handling seeds and compost. Some seeds are treated — use untreated cress.
maths_link: Measuring growth over time; angles of bending.
notes: Runs over a week, so it suits a holiday club better than a one-hour session.

steps: Line the petri dishes with damp cotton wool and scatter cress seeds evenly. | Leave them in the dark for two days to germinate. | Put one dish in all-round light, one in a box with a slit on one side, one in the dark. | Keep the cotton wool damp throughout. | Measure and photograph the seedlings every day for a week. | Record the height and the direction of bending. | Compare the three conditions.
risks: Compost and seed coatings carry bacteria and some seeds are chemically treated — untreated cress only, and hands washed afterwards. | The cardboard box on a sunny windowsill blocks the walkway — it goes at the back of the sill, not on the floor. | Cling film over a Petri dish with condensation drips — the dish stands on a tray.
science: A shoot bends towards light because auxin, a plant hormone, collects on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more, so that side grows longer and the shoot leans over. That is phototropism, and in a shoot it is positive. In a root the same hormone has the opposite effect — it slows growth where it collects — so a root turns downwards whichever way round the seed happens to land: positive gravitropism. Which is why a dish turned on its side still sends roots down and shoots up, and why the dark dish matters: it separates bending from simply growing.

subject: Biology

safety: Outdoor risk assessment, high-vis, headcount at every stop. Wash hands afterwards. Never sample near the river edge.
maths_link: Means; scaling up a sample; area calculations; random sampling.
notes: Any park or playing field with two plainly different areas — mown and unmown, sun and shade. Uses the trundle wheel (I023) and first aid kit (I022) already on the items list.

steps: Lay two tape measures at right angles to make a grid over the sample area. | Generate random coordinates and place the quadrat there — no choosing where to put it. | Count the number of the target species inside the quadrat. | Repeat for at least ten quadrats. | Mean per quadrat x (total area / quadrat area) = population estimate. | For the transect, lay one tape from shade into open ground and place quadrats at fixed intervals. | Plot abundance against distance along the transect.

science: You cannot count every daisy in a field, so you count a known fraction and scale it up: the mean per quadrat, times the number of quadrat-sized pieces in the whole area. That only works if the quadrats go down at random, because a person choosing where to put one will choose somewhere interesting and the estimate will come out high. A transect answers a different question altogether — not how many, but how the number changes along a gradient, shade to sun or path to hedge — so there the quadrats are deliberately placed at fixed intervals rather than at random, and random placing would destroy the very thing being looked for.

name: Decay
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk.
outcome: Time for the pink colour to disappear against temperature — faster when warmer, up to the point of denaturation.
safety: Lipase and sodium carbonate are irritants. Goggles. Do not drink anything. Dispose of milk properly.
maths_link: Rate as a reciprocal; optimum temperature.
notes: The pH change is the measurable thing here, not the smell.
equipment: Fresh milk × 5 cm3|Lipase solution × 1 cm3|Sodium carbonate solution × 7 cm3|Phenolphthalein indicator × 5 drops|Water baths at a range of temperatures|Thermometer|Test tubes and rack|Dropping pipettes|Stopwatch|Eye protection
steps: Put 5 cm3 of milk, 7 cm3 of sodium carbonate and five drops of phenolphthalein in a test tube. It turns pink. | Stand the tube in the first water bath and let it reach temperature. | Add 1 cm3 of lipase and start the stopwatch. | Stop the clock when the pink colour disappears — fatty acids have made it acidic. | Repeat at each temperature, keeping every volume the same. | Rate = 1000 / time. Plot rate against temperature.
risks: Lipase and sodium carbonate solution are irritants — goggles throughout and hands washed at the end. | Water baths across a range of temperatures, the hottest of them scalding — tubes are moved with a holder and the hot bath is the tutor's. | Milk goes off and is a biological hazard once it has stood warm — it goes down the sink with plenty of water the same session, not into a bin.
science: Lipase breaks the fat in milk down into fatty acids and glycerol. The fatty acids make the mixture acidic, and phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and colourless in acid — so the moment the pink goes is the moment enough acid has been made. It is a clock for the reaction rather than a measure of how much fat is left. Warming speeds it up, because the molecules collide more often and harder, until about 40 °C; past that the lipase denatures and the rate falls away. That is why the graph peaks instead of climbing, and why it is not symmetrical: denaturing is permanent where a collision rate is not.

name: Radius of the Earth from a tall building
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate the radius of the Earth by measuring how far away the horizon is from a high vantage point.
outcome: A value for R from R = d2 / 2h, usually within 20 per cent of 6371 km.
safety: A public viewing platform only — never a roof or a window ledge. Headcount before and after. Do not lean out.
maths_link: Rearranging; standard form; percentage error; Pythagoras behind the formula.
notes: The example Halex asked for. In flat country you would use the sea horizon; in London you use the furthest identifiable landmark and accept a bigger error — which is itself the lesson.
topics: Pythagoras' Theorem, Rearranging Formulae, Standard Form, Percentages
equipment: A tall building with a public viewpoint and known height|Map or satellite view for measuring distance|Phone with a compass|Clinometer|Binoculars|Calculator|Notebook|Camera|Landmark list with known distances|Ruler
steps: Find a viewpoint of known height. A tower block whose storey count you can see works: about 3.5 m a storey. | From the top, identify the furthest landmark you can clearly see on the ground. | Measure the straight-line distance to it on a map. | That distance d, with the height h, gives R = d2 / 2h. | Convert everything to metres before substituting. | Compare with the accepted 6371 km and work out the percentage error. | Discuss why buildings and haze in London make the horizon hard to see, and what that does to d.
risks: A height with a drop — a public viewing platform with a barrier only, never a roof, a window ledge or a fire escape, and nobody leans on or over the rail. | A group in a public building — headcount before going up and again before leaving, and a meeting point agreed at the bottom first. | Binoculars pointed at the sun blind permanently — the horizon only, and it is said out loud before they are handed over. | Dropped equipment from height hits somebody below — the clinometer and the phone go on wrist straps or stay in a pocket.
science: The horizon is the place where your line of sight just grazes the curve of the Earth — so that line is a tangent, and a tangent meets the radius at 90°. Pythagoras on that right-angled triangle gives (R + h)² = R² + d², and expanding leaves 2Rh + h² = d². For any building h² is tiny against 2Rh, so it is dropped and R = d²/2h. The whole method depends on the Earth being curved: on a flat one the horizon would be infinitely far away whatever your height, which is what makes this worth measuring rather than reading.

name: Eratosthenes’ shadow
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate the circumference of the Earth from the length of a shadow at midday.
outcome: A circumference within about 10 per cent of 40 000 km.
safety: Sun safety — hats, shade, and never look at the sun. Chalk marks only on your own ground.
maths_link: Trigonometry; ratio and proportion; angles in parallel lines.
notes: Two schools in different cities measuring on the same day is the classic version. Published data works if you only have one site.
topics: Right-Angled Trigonometry, Ratio Problems, Angles in Parallel Lines
equipment: Metre stick or tall vertical pole|Spirit level|Tape measure|Chalk|Protractor|Calculator|Clock set to local solar noon|Published shadow data from a second latitude|Notebook|Camera
steps: Stand the metre stick perfectly vertical on flat ground and check with the level. | About 15 minutes before local solar noon, mark the shadow tip every few minutes. | The shortest shadow is solar noon. | Measure the shortest shadow length and the stick height. | Angle = inverse tan (shadow / height). That is your angle from the sun. | Get the same angle for the same day from a place at a different latitude. | Difference in angles / 360 = distance between the places / circumference. | Rearrange for circumference.
risks: Working in direct sun for the middle of the day — hats, water, shade between readings, and the session is moved if it is very hot. | Looking at the sun to line the pole up blinds — the SHADOW is measured and the sun is never looked at, which is said before the pole goes up. | A metre stick standing vertically falls on somebody — it is held or based in something heavy, not balanced. | Chalk marks on ground that is not yours — a playground or your own path only.
science: Sunlight reaches the Earth in rays that are effectively parallel, because the sun is so far away. Two places at different latitudes therefore cast shadows at different angles at the same moment, and the difference between those two angles is exactly the angle between the two places as seen from the centre of the Earth — which is angles in parallel lines, and nothing more. So the difference in angle is the same fraction of 360° as the distance between the places is of the whole circumference. Eratosthenes did this around 240 BC with a well and a stick and came within a few per cent.

variables: The latitude of the second place|The date, which changes how high the sun gets|The height of the stick|How carefully solar noon is found

name: Height of a tree or tower by clinometer
subject: Maths
aim: Measure the height of something too tall to reach using an angle and a distance.

name: Speed of light with a microwave and chocolate
subject: Physics
aim: Measure the speed of light using standing waves in a microwave oven.
outcome: A value near 3 x 10^8 m/s from c = 2 d f.
safety: Adult operates the microwave. Melted chocolate is hot. Remove the turntable first, and do not run the oven empty.
maths_link: Standard form; unit prefixes; v = f λ.
notes: The single best "the maths is real" demonstration for a reluctant student. Needs a microwave, so it suits a holiday event at the community centre.
topics: Waves, Standard Form, Units & Measures, Substitution

steps: Take the turntable out so the food cannot rotate. | Lay the chocolate flat on the plate and put it in the oven. | Heat for 20 seconds — just long enough for the first melted patches to appear. | Measure the distance between the centres of two adjacent melted patches. That is half a wavelength. | Wavelength = 2 x that distance. | Read the frequency off the back of the oven, usually 2450 MHz. | c = f x wavelength. Compare with 3 x 10^8 m/s. | Then eat the evidence.

science: A microwave oven does not heat evenly. The waves reflect off the metal walls and interfere with themselves, making a standing wave with fixed hot spots where the wave is strongest and cold spots where it cancels; the turntable exists to carry food through them. Take it out and the hot spots stay put and melt the chocolate in a pattern. Adjacent melted patches are HALF a wavelength apart, because a standing wave has two antinodes to a wavelength. With the frequency printed on the back of the oven, c = fλ, and the answer lands near 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

name: Buffon’s needle
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate π by dropping matchsticks on to a set of parallel lines.
outcome: An estimate of π that improves visibly as the number of drops rises.
safety: None. Use matchsticks with the heads removed, or cocktail sticks with blunted ends.
maths_link: Experimental probability; convergence; why large samples matter.
notes: Pool the whole group’s results to get to 1000 drops. The convergence graph is the real lesson.

steps: Rule parallel lines on the paper exactly one stick-length apart. | Drop the sticks on to the paper from a small height, one at a time or a handful at once. | Count the total dropped, N, and the number crossing a line, C. | π is approximately 2N / C. | Do 50 drops, then 100, then 500, pooling results across the group. | Plot the estimate against the number of drops. | Watch it converge — and note how slowly.

science: Drop a needle whose length equals the line spacing and the chance it crosses a line works out at 2/π. It falls out of two things being random and independent: where the centre of the needle lands between the lines, and what angle it happens to lie at. Integrating over both gives 2/π, so counting crossings and rearranging estimates π. The estimate wanders a long way early on and settles slowly — the error falls roughly as 1/√N, so a hundred times as many drops buys only ten times the accuracy, which is the real lesson here about experimental probability.

name: Monte Carlo π with rice
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate π by scattering grains over a square with a quarter circle drawn in it.
outcome: π approximately 4 x (grains inside the arc / grains in total).
safety: Sweep up afterwards. Do not use rice with anyone who has a grain allergy — dried peas work too.
maths_link: Area ratios; proportion; estimation.
notes: Uses the pair of compasses (I007) for the arc. Pairs well with PR-FN05 in the same session.

steps: Draw a square on the card and, from one corner, a quarter circle with radius equal to the side. | Stand the card in the tray. | Scatter rice evenly over the whole square from a height. | Count the grains inside the arc and the total on the card. | π is approximately 4 x inside / total. | Repeat with more grains and see the estimate settle. | Compare the accuracy with Buffon’s needle for the same effort.

name: π from circles
subject: Maths
aim: Discover π as the gradient of circumference plotted against diameter.
outcome: A straight line through the origin with a gradient of about 3.14.
safety: None.
maths_link: Gradient; direct proportion; line of best fit; constants in maths.
notes: The moment a ten-year-old sees π appear from measuring jam jars is worth the whole session.
topics: Area & Circumference of Circles, Straight Line Graphs, Direct Proportion, Scatter Graphs & Correlation
equipment: Round objects of different sizes × 10|String or a flexible tape measure|30 cm ruler|Graph paper|Pencil|Calculator|Results table|Scissors|Whiteboard|Marker
steps: Wrap the string once round each object and mark where it meets. | Straighten the string against the ruler to get the circumference. | Measure the diameter across the widest point. | Record both for all ten objects. | Plot circumference against diameter. | Draw the line of best fit through the origin. | Measure its gradient. That is π. | Divide C by d for each object as a check.
risks: Nothing beyond ordinary classroom care — scissors are the only sharp thing and they are passed handle-first. | Round objects roll off a table and break — they are kept on a tray rather than at the edge.
science: Every circle has the same ratio of circumference to diameter, whatever its size — that ratio is π, and the fact that it is constant is the whole point. Plot C against d for ten different objects and the points lie on a straight line through the origin, because C = πd is a direct proportion; the gradient is π. Dividing C by d for each object gets the same number a different way, and the two agreeing is what shows the measuring was honest: a line of best fit forgives one bad point, and a column of ratios does not.
log: The circumference of each object|The diameter of each object|C ÷ d for each one|The gradient of the line of best fit
variables: The objects measured, and how wide a range of sizes they cover|How the circumference is measured — string, tape, or rolling|How carefully the widest point is found|The number of objects

name: Monty Hall
subject: Maths
aim: Test whether switching doors really doubles your chance of winning.
outcome: Switching wins about two thirds of the time over 100+ trials.
safety: None.
maths_link: Conditional probability; relative frequency; why intuition fails.
notes: The argument it starts is the point. Have the simulation ready for the student who refuses to believe the cups.
equipment: Cups or cards × 3|A counter or sweet to hide|Tally sheet|Whiteboard|Marker|Calculator|Timer|Tablet for a simulation to compare against|Pen|Results poster
steps: One person hides the counter under one of three cups while the other looks away. | The player picks a cup without lifting it. | The host lifts one of the other two cups, always revealing an empty one. | The player either sticks or switches. Record the choice and the result. | Do 50 trials always sticking, then 50 always switching. | Compare the two win rates. | Run a simulation for 10 000 trials and compare with your 100.
risks: Nothing physical at all — the sweet used as the prize is the only thing to check, so it goes nowhere near anyone with an allergy to it and is not eaten.
science: Your first pick has a 1 in 3 chance of being right, so the other two cups hold 2 in 3 between them. The host then lifts one of those two — and crucially he knows where the counter is and always lifts an empty one, so he has not shown you a random cup. The two thirds does not spread back over all three; it collects on the single unlifted cup you did not pick. So switching wins two thirds of the time and sticking wins one third. Intuition insists it must be even because two cups are left, and running it a hundred times is the answer to that.
log: Wins and losses when sticking|Wins and losses when switching|The win rate for each, as a fraction|How close each is to 1/3 and 2/3 after 50, after 100, after 10 000
variables: Whether the player sticks or switches|The number of trials|The number of cups — try it with ten|Whether the host knows where the counter is, which is the assumption the whole thing rests on

name: Perimeter of a park with a trundle wheel
subject: Maths
aim: Measure the perimeter of a real park and estimate its area.
outcome: A perimeter in metres and an area estimate, checked against a satellite measurement.
safety: Outdoor risk assessment, high-vis, headcount at every corner. Stay away from the river bank.
maths_link: Perimeter; compound area; scale drawings; estimation.
notes: Uses the trundle wheel, tape measure, cones and first aid kit already on the items list.
topics: Perimeter, Area of 2-D Shapes, Scale Drawings & Maps, Estimation
equipment: Trundle wheel|30 m tape measure|Clipboard and recording sheet|Map or printed satellite image|Pencil|Calculator|High-vis vests|First aid kit|Cones to mark corners|Camera
steps: Print a satellite image of the park and mark the corners on it. | Walk the perimeter with the trundle wheel, recording each straight section separately. | Add the sections for the total perimeter. | Sketch the park as a set of rectangles and triangles on the map. | Measure the sides of each shape by pacing or by scaling off the map. | Calculate the area of each shape and add them. | Compare with the area given by an online map tool and discuss the difference.
risks: An outdoor session in a public park — written outdoor risk assessment, high-vis, and a headcount at every corner as well as before leaving. | The river bank is the drowning risk — the route is walked on the path side and the corner nearest the water is measured from the path. | Traffic on the park entrances — the group crosses together at one point agreed beforehand. | A trundle wheel takes eyes down to the ground — whoever is wheeling has a partner watching ahead for them.
science: A trundle wheel counts revolutions and one click is one circumference, usually exactly a metre — which is why the wheel is about 318 mm across, since C = πd. Perimeter is the distance round the edge and area is what is enclosed, and the two are not tied together: two shapes with the same perimeter can have very different areas, which is exactly why the area has to be built up out of rectangles and triangles rather than guessed at from the walk. Every measurement carries an error and the errors add along the way, so the total perimeter is less precise than any single section of it.
log: The length of each straight section|The total perimeter|The area of each rectangle and triangle|The total area, against a satellite measurement
variables: Where exactly the boundary is taken to be|How the park is cut into shapes for the area|Who walks it, and how straight they walk|Whether curved edges are walked or approximated by straight sections

name: Flow rate of a river
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate how much water passes a point on a river every second.
outcome: A flow rate in cubic metres per second, from area x velocity.
safety: Never enter the water. Measure from a bridge or a fenced bank only. One adult per three students at the water’s edge. Wash hands afterwards.
maths_link: Means; compound measures; cross-sectional area; cubic metres per second.
notes: Pick the stretch before the session and check the bank is fenced or gently shelving. Surface floats travel faster than the average, so the answer is always an overestimate. That is a discussion, not a flaw.
topics: Compound Measures, Mean, Area of 2-D Shapes, Volume & Surface Area
equipment: Oranges or tennis balls as floats × 2|Stopwatch|30 m tape measure|Metre stick for depth (used from a bridge)|Clipboard and waterproof sheet|Calculator|High-vis vests|First aid kit|Camera|Map of the reach
steps: Pick a straight stretch of the river with a bridge or a safe fenced bank. | Measure a 10 m length along the bank and mark both ends. | Drop a float in at the upstream mark and time it to the downstream mark. | Repeat five times and take a mean. Velocity = distance / mean time. | Measure the width, and the depth at three or four points across it. | Cross-sectional area = width x mean depth. | Flow rate = area x velocity, in cubic metres per second. | Compare with the Environment Agency gauging figure for that river, if it has one.
risks: Moving water — nobody enters it, at all, and every measurement is taken from a bridge or a fenced bank. | The water's edge is the one place a slip is serious — one adult per three students at the edge, and the floats are thrown rather than placed. | River water carries bacteria including leptospirosis — no hands in the water, cuts covered, hands washed before anybody eats. | Leaning over a bridge parapet to watch a float — the metre stick is used to point rather than to reach, and nobody climbs the rail.
science: Flow rate is volume per second, and it is the cross-sectional area of the river multiplied by how fast the water is moving: Q = Av. The units carry the argument — m² × m/s is m³/s. A float only measures the surface, and water at the surface moves faster than water dragging along the bed, so the true mean velocity is around 85 per cent of the float speed; ignore that and the answer comes out high. The depth varies across the channel too, so several readings are meaned rather than one taken in the middle.
log: The time for the float over 10 m, five times|The mean velocity|The width, and the depths across the channel|The flow rate in m³/s, against the published figure
variables: Where on the river the measurement is taken|The length of the timed stretch|The number of depth readings taken across the channel|Whether the surface-speed correction is applied
